settings.heading: What experts say
settings.intro: Heat and massage are the two halves of what Jointwell does. Here is what clinicians say about those two things in general — their words, not ours, and none of them are talking about our product.
settings.footnote: Jointwell is a comfort device. It isn't a medical treatment and doesn't cure, treat or prevent any condition. Keep doing what your GP and physio have told you to do.

settings.role: nhs.uk, on easing joint stiffness at home
settings.quote: Heat applied to the affected area can be very effective in reducing pain.

settings.text: Heat-pack guidance says apply warmth for 15 to 20 minutes. A hot water bottle holds useful warmth for 20 to 30 minutes and a microwaved wheat bag about 30. The dose in your cupboard is roughly right. It's the delivery that runs out.
Knees, shoulders and elbows sit under thin skin with little muscle or fat around them, so they lose warmth faster than the rest of you and hold it worst. Cold hands, cold nose, cold knees.

NICE, which writes the guidance the NHS follows, puts exercise, weight management and information first for osteoarthritis. We aren't a substitute for any of that. Warmth is what people use to get moving in the morning so they can do the rest.
settings.source: NICE guideline NG226, Osteoarthritis in over 16s (2022)

settings.intro: Straight answers. If yours isn't here, ring us.

settings.question: Isn't this just a heating pad with extra steps?
settings.answer: A heating pad gives you heat that fades, or heat that ties you to a wall socket. Jointwell holds whichever of the five levels you pick, 45°C to 65°C, for a full 30 minutes. It adds vibration massage at three strengths, straps on so it stays put, and runs cordless in any chair in the house.

settings.question: Will it work for me? My joints have been like this a long time.
settings.answer: It isn't a cure and we won't pretend otherwise. Nobody can promise what it will do for your joint. What we can promise is warmth at the level you choose, held for thirty minutes, with massage alongside it. The 90-day trial is there so your own knee gets the deciding vote rather than our copy.

settings.question: Will it fit me?
settings.answer: One size, 46 cm across and 30 cm tall, with a 55 cm strap span. It fits either knee, and the extension strap in the box takes it round a shoulder or up an arm to the elbow. If it doesn't fit you, the 90-day trial covers a full refund and we pay the return postage.

settings.question: Is it safe? Will it burn me?
settings.answer:
Heat can burn skin if it is too hot, held too long, or used by someone who can't feel it properly. So: start at level 1 or 2 (45 to 50°C), wear it over clothing rather than bare skin, and only go higher if it stays comfortable. Every session ends itself after 30 minutes, so it can't be left running, and you can stop it at any point.

Don't use it while asleep, over broken skin, or on a joint that's hot, red and swollen. If you have diabetes, circulation problems, reduced feeling in your skin, or you're under medical care for that joint, ask your GP before using any heat product. If the skin goes red and stays red after you take it off, that level is too high for you.

settings.question: When will it arrive?
settings.answer: We dispatch within 1 to 3 working days and most orders arrive 7 to 10 working days after you order, occasionally up to 14. Every parcel is tracked and we email you the link the moment it leaves. Your ninety days don't start until it's in your hands.

settings.question: How do I know this isn't another Facebook gadget?
settings.answer: Fair question, because this market is full of them. We dispatch most orders within 1 to 3 working days and track every one. There's a UK returns address, UK support, a 2-year warranty, and a 90-day trial where we pay the postage back. The reviews on this page are from customers with an order on file, in their own words. Junk sellers can't afford the guarantee.

settings.question: Can I use it after a knee replacement?
settings.answer: Ask your surgeon or physio first, and follow what they say. Many people are told heat is fine once the wound has fully healed, but that's their call, not ours. If they say yes, most people use it as the warm half hour before their exercises.

settings.question: How do I charge it, and how long does a charge last?
settings.answer: It charges over USB-C with the cable in the box, the same cable as most phones. It has a 3000 mAh battery. The panel shows the battery level.

settings.question: What happens if I send it back?
settings.answer: Email us within 90 days of delivery. We send you a UK returns address and a postage label. Post it back, and we refund what you paid in full once it arrives. You don't pay the postage and you don't have to give a reason, though we would like to hear it.

settings.question: Who shouldn't use it?
settings.answer: Anyone who has been told to avoid heat on that joint. If you have diabetes, circulation problems, reduced feeling in your skin, a pacemaker, an unhealed wound or a joint that's hot, red and swollen, talk to your GP before using any heat product. Don't use it while asleep, over broken skin, or on a child. If you're pregnant or under medical care for the joint, ask first. It's a comfort device, not a treatment, and your GP's word beats ours.

settings.heading: It starts with the stairs. It never stays there.
settings.intro: If any of this sounds familiar, keep reading.

settings.shot: Stairs, shot from the bottom looking up. Hand on the banister in the corner of frame.
settings.lines:
Sideways?
One step at a time?
Maybe even on your hands and knees?

settings.shot: Armchair, side-on. A woman leaning forward, hand on the arm, about to stand.
settings.lines:
You work out how you'll get up before you've sat down.
It used to be where you relaxed.

settings.shot: Open car door in a supermarket car park. One foot on the ground, one still inside.
settings.lines:
That pause before you put your weight on it.
Hoping nobody's watching.

settings.shot: Overgrown garden through a kitchen window. Mug on the sill.
settings.lines:
Too much kneeling.
Too much bending.
You don't want it to, but the grass gets longer every day.

settings.shot: Dark bedroom, someone lying on their back, ceiling.
settings.lines:
You've stopped sleeping on that side.
Then the other side started too.

Everyone your age has a knee.
So you don't mention it.
You just plan around it.

settings.heading: Then you go to the GP.
settings.intro: Everyone does their best. It still isn't enough.

settings.shot: GP waiting room. Row of chairs, the ticket screen, a poster about flu jabs.
settings.lines:
You put it off. It's only a knee.
When you finally go, you get eight minutes.

settings.shot: A hand pressing on a knee. Clinical, close, cropped.
settings.lines:
Wear and tear, they say.
Very common.
Paracetamol, keep it moving, lose a bit if you can.

settings.shot: A brown NHS envelope on a doormat.
settings.lines:
The physio letter takes ten weeks.
Six sessions.
A sheet of exercises for the landing carpet.

settings.shot: Printed exercise sheet, folded, on a kitchen table. Coffee ring on it.
settings.lines:
The physio is lovely.
The exercises hurt.
By session four you've stopped, and neither of you mentions it.

settings.shot: A syringe on a tray, out of focus.
settings.lines:
So it's the injection.
And it works. Properly works.
For about ten weeks.

settings.shot: A calendar page with a date circled.
settings.lines:
Then one morning it's back.
"We can only do that a few times a year."
"Have you thought about a replacement?"

Referred. Not booked.
A letter. A consultation. A list.
Nobody says how long the list is.
You look it up and wish you hadn't.

settings.shot: Three boxes on a bedside table. Co-codamol, naproxen, paracetamol. Labels visible.
settings.lines:
One leaves you foggy.
One upsets your stomach.
One is fine. It's just not enough any more.

None of this is anyone's fault.
The GP has eight minutes. The physio has six sessions. The surgeon has a list.
It's just that nobody's job is to get you up the stairs this month.

settings.text: That's the bit Paula got tired of waiting for.

settings.lines:
Paula did all of this for four years.
Then she found something that took thirty minutes a morning and stayed in the cupboard for a week before she tried it.
First, though, the GP.

settings.quote: I found it in a Facebook group for osteoarthritis. At first I was sceptical. Was it really going to do anything? I had already tried the lot. Then I saw the 90-day guarantee, a 90-day trial they called it: if it doesn't work, send it back. So I thought, go on then, what is there to lose.

settings.lines:
Properly warm, right into the joint. The squeezing I wasn't expecting. It was like someone's hands.
It felt good while it was on.
I'd had nice before, though.

I'd started doing it first thing, on the edge of the bed with the radio on.
The mornings weren't as stiff.
I put it down to the weather.

I went up the stairs with the washing and didn't hold on.
I only noticed at the top.
I stood there a bit.

I did the borders in the garden. Not all of them.
But you could tell from the kitchen window.

Thirty minutes, first thing, same as brushing my teeth.
My sister asked what I'd been doing differently.
That's when I told her about the gadget.

Thirty minutes with it on, whenever it suited her, and she got on with her day.
If you recognised the stairs, the chair, the garden through the window, you're where she was at the start.
The device is the same one she's still using.
Another winter of the stairs, or thirty minutes tomorrow morning. The wrap costs less than the cupboard did.
